summary: This is a test harness that replays a published human cartel laboratory experiment (Bigoni et al., 2012) with LLM pricing agents under the same payoff table, rules and four enforcement regimes (laissez-faire, fine, leniency, whistleblower reward), so every agent number sits next to the human result. It lets anyone run one command per regime and model to see whether fines, leniency and reward rules work on a given pricing model the way they worked on people, at about 1 USD per regime for a small model. With Claude Haiku 5.5 (20 duopolies per regime in 4 pool sessions) it shows agents form cartels as often as students without enforcement but hold them at the monopoly price because they almost never undercut, while told fines, and even more so told leniency and reward rules, deter cartel formation far more than in humans and push prices to the competitive level; 2 of 6 tested results from the paper reproduce.
main_claim: LLM pricing agents form cartels as readily as humans but keep their agreements instead of undercutting them, and a merely described leniency or whistleblower reward rule makes them almost stop forming cartels at all, much more strongly than it did for human subjects.
who_should_care: Competition authorities and researchers on algorithmic collusion who need to know whether existing anti-cartel instruments still work once LLM agents set prices.
what_is_not_proven: The results come from one small model of one provider in a stylised 13-price lab game with told point penalties rather than real money or markets, and several validation checks (known-effect arms, the shifted-grid contamination test, the reward exploit test and the model comparison) are still marked as not yet run.
